content_voiceover: Here's the classic three phase indirect Coombs test. Phase one, immediate spin at room temperature, mainly picks up IgM antibodies. Phase two, 37 degree incubation in albumin or LISS, favors IgG antibody binding. Phase three, the AHG phase, involves washing the cells three times to remove unbound globulins, adding antihuman globulin reagent, spinning, and reading for agglutination, which means IgG is bound to the red cell surface. This method is time-consuming and technique-dependent, which is why gel and polybrene methods were developed as faster alternatives. Look at the example: screening cell I is negative at immediate spin and 37 degrees, but 2 plus positive at the AHG phase, while SII and SIII stay negative throughout. That pattern means the patient has an IgG antibody against an antigen present on SI but absent from SII and SIII, only detectable after the AHG step.
keypoints: Three phases: immediate spin (IgM), 37C incubation (favors IgG), then AHG phase.
AHG phase = wash x3, add AHG reagent, spin, and read agglutination for bound IgG.
Method is time and skill intensive, hence gel and polybrene alternatives exist.
Positive only at AHG phase (like SI at 2+) means an IgG alloantibody detected only after the antiglobulin step.
